A1.justification: The PDFs describe the same mini-batch selection research, despite the changed title and SSM/CoLM terminology. Both versions' complete text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original Phi-2 fine-tuning experiments on MathInstruct, including six mathematical evaluation datasets, training-time comparisons and ablations.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments with Phi-2, Phi-3 and Zephyr, mathematical and classification tasks, selection baselines and component analyses.

M1.justification: SSM's inverse-source-size sampling and batch-wide selection become CoLM's retention of all small-source examples within each candidate batch and separate selection from large sources. v2 adds Adam-history-normalized gradients, source-specific sparsification masks and clustering to infer unspecified sources. Zeroth-order V-projection gradients and uniform selected-example weights are retained.

E1.justification: The MathInstruct training dataset and six mathematical evaluation datasets are retained. v2 adds SST-2, CB and MultiRC classification experiments, including data without supplied source labels (Sections 5.1 and 5.4, Table 7). This substantially broadens task coverage.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's random small- and large-batch training comparisons, v2 Table 1 evaluates Big Loss, Grad Norm, Middle Perplexity, Completion Length, Least Confidence and hidden-state facility-location selection. These are actual additional comparators; FT denotes the retained random-batch training baseline.

E3.justification: The existing Phi-2 mathematical training and decoding settings largely remain unchanged. Added experiments introduce Phi-3 training for 4K iterations, Zephyr training for 2K iterations, batch-size-256 comparisons and additional CoLM batch sizes. Classification uses 250 CB examples or 3K SST-2/MultiRC examples, 80 iterations, a 20-iteration clustering warm-up and four clustering updates.

E4.justification: The weighted-sampling ablation is replaced by component tests of small-source retention, separate source selection and Adam normalization. v2 also examines weighting and distance choices, extends sparsification tests, and adds gradient-approximation and layer comparisons, gradient-variance measurements, batch-size sensitivity, completion-length analysis and alternative clustering procedures (Tables 2–7; Figures 3 and 5).

E5.justification: Both versions specify three experimental repetitions and report ± values in tables. However, v1 Figure 1 includes error bars on convergence curves, whereas the replacement convergence plot in v2 Figure 3a omits them. No increase in repetitions or new significance-testing procedure is documented.

E6.justification: For Phi-2 at 1K iterations, Table 1 replaces SSM's 54.0 average accuracy with 56.6 for the revised CoLM method; matched random-batch results remain 50.1 and 52.6. v1's 2K SSM results are absent. Numerous baseline, model, classification and ablation results are added. Table 7 reports 75.8 for online clustering and 81.9 for fine-tuned-model clustering, versus 78.9 for larger-batch FT.

T1.justification: v1's conditional nonconvex-SGD convergence theorem and Appendix A proof are replaced. v2 introduces dense-region, Lipschitz and boundedness assumptions, source-size and local-medoid statements, and a variance-reduction theorem (Theorems 4.1–4.3), supported by new lemmas and derivations in Appendix A.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes memory-efficient gradient matching and its convergence benefits. v2 centers its contributions on overcoming source imbalance and Adam-specific selection problems, while extending applicability claims to additional models and classification tasks. It additionally claims superiority to four-times-larger batches and 2.7x speedups under the expanded comparison settings.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations concerning unreliable small-source medoids and the need to match Adam-normalized gradients. It attributes superiority over larger batches despite higher gradient variance to more uniform learning across sources (Section 5.2). Section 5.4 newly discusses the dependence of source-free application on clustering quality and proposes using a fine-tuned proxy model.

D1.justification: Most existing learning-rate, sequence-length, LoRA, hardware and decoding details are retained, with material relocated to Appendix B. v2 adds Zephyr-specific LoRA target modules, explicit clustering warm-up/update details, the small-source threshold and a reference identifying the memory-efficient random-projection implementation.

R1.justification: The related-work organization is retained, but v2 adds completion-length selection, Big Loss, projection, model and benchmark references. It foregrounds prior mini-batch coreset work as its starting point and removes v1's blanket assertion that existing selection methods cannot provide theoretical guarantees. Several older optimization-background citations are also removed.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contribution narrative and substantial portions of the method exposition are rewritten. The problem formulation becomes a gradient-matching preliminary section, and the method is reorganized around imbalance, Adam and dimensionality. Training details and pseudocode move to separate appendices, replacing the previous single-proof appendix structure.

P2.justification: v2 restructures Table 1 around additional comparators, replaces the weighted-sampling table and adds Tables 5–7. Performance and timing plots are redesigned, the two convergence panels become one, and new illustrative, multi-model, variance, batch-size, source-distribution and completion-length graphics appear. Pseudocode is reformatted and relocated to Appendix C.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical validation: Table 1 tests alternative selection methods, Tables 2 and 5–6 examine the proposed components, and additional models and classification tasks test broader applicability. This provides materially stronger evidence for the method's advantages and dependencies. Missing convergence error bars and the dependence of larger-batch superiority on fine-tuned-model clustering in Table 7 temper the gains but do not outweigh the stronger empirical support.
